# solo-msa_v2-gemini-3-8-flash-flash-saturation-low-nostepcounter

<!-- Generated by tools/export_results.py. Edit only the Experiment and Observations sections. -->

## Experiment

Repeats [`solo-msa_v2-gemini-3-8-flash-flash-saturation-low`](../solo-msa_v2-gemini-3-8-flash-flash-saturation-low/summary.md) (`solo`, `gemini-3.8-flash` at `low` thinking, 500 steps, compaction at 64K tokens, `$40` per-agent cost cap, 50-pair `flash` subset) with one change: the per-turn step counter ("Step n of 500: k left") is turned off. With 100-step budgets the counter raised `solo` from 0 to 1 of 10 pairs to 7 of 10 on `flash_10`. This run checks whether it still matters when the budget is large enough that agents rarely run out, to decide whether the counter should be part of the standard setup. It ran as two 25-pair halves on two API keys and was merged into this one run.

## Observations

- 32/50 (64%) without the step counter vs. 36/50 (72%) with it, at the same cost (`$25.64` vs. `$25.70`). Pair by pair, 32 passed in both runs, 14 failed in both, 4 passed only with the counter, and none passed only without it. A 4-to-0 split on 50 pairs is not statistically significant on its own (exact two-sided test, p = 0.125).
- Step use was almost identical: median 84 steps per pair in both runs, and 22 passes in each run finished within 100 steps. Every agent submitted.
- One of the 4 losses was a budget failure the counter prevents: on `pillow_task/290` (3,5) the agent used all 500 steps without knowing how close it was to the limit, while with the counter it finished in 180 steps and passed. The other 3 (`pallets_click_task/2956` (1,8), `pallets_jinja_task/1621` (4,5) and (4,10)) were submitted on time with one feature failing its hidden tests, which looks like ordinary run-to-run variation.
- Together with the 100-step results, where the counter is the largest single improvement measured, this supports keeping the step counter in the standard setup: it costs nothing, prevents budget failures, and did not hurt any pair here.
